lesson.title: Electric Charge: The Property Behind Every Circuit
lesson.summary: This section introduces electric charge as a fundamental, quantized property of matter, explains why like charges repel and unlike charges attract, and shows with real numbers just how strong the electric force can be.
lesson.body:
Everything you'll study in circuits starts from one basic fact about matter: some particles carry a property called electric charge, and that property comes in exactly two flavors, which we call positive and negative. Protons carry positive charge, electrons carry negative charge, and neutrons carry none. An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons has no net charge ,  it's electrically neutral ,  but if it gains or loses electrons, it becomes charged. This is why charge, unlike mass, can be either sign: it's not just "how much stuff," it's "how much of which kind."

Charge doesn't come in arbitrary amounts. It's quantized, meaning every charged object carries a whole-number multiple of a smallest possible unit, the elementary charge, worth about 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs. The coulomb (C) is the standard unit for measuring charge, and it's a large amount compared to the elementary charge ,  one coulomb corresponds to roughly 6.24×10¹⁸ electrons' worth of charge. So when a wire "carries charge," what's physically happening is enormous numbers of electrons shifting position, each one contributing that same tiny fixed amount.

A second key fact is that charge is conserved: it can move from one place to another, but it cannot be created or destroyed. When you rub a balloon on your hair, you're not manufacturing charge out of nothing ,  electrons are being physically transferred from the hair onto the balloon, leaving the hair short some electrons (net positive) and the balloon with extra electrons (net negative). Every electron that leaves one object shows up on the other; the total charge across both objects before and after is exactly the same.

Charge is significant because charges exert forces on each other, and the rule is simple: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. This isn't arbitrary ,  it reflects the fact that there really are two distinct kinds of charge whose interaction depends on sign. The strength of that force depends on how much charge is involved and how far apart the charges are, growing rapidly as the distance shrinks. To get a feel for the scale, consider two small objects each carrying 1 microcoulomb of charge (1×10⁻⁶ C), held 1 centimeter apart. Using the relationship F = k·q₁q₂/r², with k ≈ 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², the force between them works out to about 90 newtons ,  comparable to the weight of a 9 kilogram object, from charges you can't even see. This tells you that electric forces, at the scale of individual charges, are extraordinarily strong, which is exactly why even a slight imbalance of electrons can push or pull other charges into motion.

That pushing and pulling is the seed of everything a circuit does: batteries, wires, and components exist to control the arrangement and motion of charge. Before you can make sense of current, voltage, or any circuit behavior, you need this foundation ,  charge as a real, conserved, quantized property carried by particles, capable of exerting force on other charge at a distance.
